## Why the Sky Is Blue

Sunlight contains all visible wavelengths, and when it enters the atmosphere it collides with gas molecules (primarily nitrogen and oxygen) that are much smaller than the wavelength of light. These molecules scatter the incoming light in all directions, but they do so much more efficiently at shorter wavelengths than at longer ones—a phenomenon called **Rayleigh scattering**. Because blue and violet light have the shortest wavelengths in the visible spectrum, they are scattered far more strongly than red or orange light, filling the sky with diffuse blue light that reaches our eyes from every direction. (The sky appears blue rather than violet even though violet is scattered even more, because the Sun emits less violet light and our eyes are simply more sensitive to blue.)

## Rayleigh Scattering Wavelength Dependence

The intensity of scattered light is inversely proportional to the **fourth power of the wavelength**:

$$I \propto \frac{1}{\lambda^4}$$

This strong wavelength dependence means that halving the wavelength increases the scattered intensity by a factor of $2^4 = 16$. This is precisely why blue light (~450 nm) scatters roughly $(700/450)^4 \approx 6$ times more than red light (~700 nm), producing the blue sky—and the same physics explains why sunsets appear red, as the longer path length through the atmosphere removes most of the scattered blue, leaving the transmitted red light.
